questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: compute the change in the net capital stock
questions.stem: A bakery's ovens were bought for 80 thousand and are now worth 60 thousand. This year it spends 30 thousand on a new oven. What is the change in its net capital stock this year?

options.text: +10 thousand, adding the 30 and subtracting the 20 of wear
+30 thousand, counting only the new oven purchase
options.misconception: ignores depreciation and treats all investment as a stock increase

options.text: +50 thousand, adding the purchase to the 20 of lost value
options.misconception: adds depreciation to investment instead of subtracting it

options.text: -20 thousand, letting the wear exceed the new purchase
options.misconception: measures the stock change from wear alone and ignores the purchase

questions.explanation: The capital stock is a stock, so it rises by investment and falls by depreciation: 30 − 20 = +10 thousand. Counting only the purchase ignores that 20 thousand of value has already worn away, and adding the 20 instead of subtracting it treats wear as a second gift of capital, while reporting only the wear forgets the oven the bakery actually bought.
questions.hint: A stock changes by what flows in, minus what flows out.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: compute net investment from gross investment and depreciation
questions.stem: A manufacturer's net capital stock was 1,000 million at the start of the year. Depreciation runs at 5 percent of the stock, and gross investment this year is 240 million. What is net investment this year? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Depreciation is the rate applied to the opening stock, 0.05 × 1,000 = 50, so net investment is 240 − 50 = 190 million. Using gross investment alone overstates the addition to productive capacity by the whole 50 of wear, and netting depreciation out a second time would charge the firm for capital it never bought.
questions.hint: Depreciation is the rate times the stock you started the year with.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: convert net investment into a share of output
questions.stem: An economy has output of 12,000 billion. Gross investment is 3,000 billion and depreciation is 600 billion. What is the net investment rate, as a share of output?

options.misconception: keeps gross rather than net investment in the numerator
mistakes the depreciation share for the net investment rate
divides depreciation by investment instead of by output

questions.explanation: Net investment is gross investment less depreciation, 3,000 − 600 = 2,400, and the rate is 2,400 ÷ 12,000 = 0.20, that is 20 percent of output. Keeping 3,000 in the numerator gives 25 and answers a different question, how much was bought rather than how much the stock grew, while 600 ÷ 12,000 gives the 15 percent of output lost to wear, and 600 ÷ 3,000 gives the 5 percent that has no economic meaning at all because the two are not shares of anything common.
questions.hint: Build the numerator first, then divide by output.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: distinguish adding land from adding inputs per acre
questions.stem: A farm can raise output by ploughing more acres or by applying more fertilizer to the acres it already farms. Which statement describes the second of those two routes?

options.text: Intensive margin, since the same land yields more per hectare
Extensive margin, since the same inputs yield more per hectare
options.misconception: labels a rise in output per acre as a change in the extensive margin

options.text: Intensive margin, since more land is brought under cultivation
options.misconception: confuses adding inputs per acre with adding acres of land

options.text: Extensive margin, since each hectare yields more output
options.misconception: pairs the wrong margin with the correct per-hectare result

questions.explanation: Holding the land fixed and raising what each hectare produces is the intensive margin, and 12 percent more from the same acreage is an intensive gain even though no new field is opened. The belief that adding hectares is the intensive route reverses the definitions, and the two options that pair the intensive label with new land or the extensive label with more output per hectare are the standard swap errors.
questions.hint: Ask whether the number of acres changed or the yield per acre did.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: identify capital deepening in a concrete hiring decision
questions.stem: A firm buys one robot that performs the work two machine operators used to do, and lays off both operators. What has happened to capital per worker?

options.text: It rose, because the workforce shrank while the tool base grew
It fell, because headcount fell while the tool base was unchanged
options.misconception: ignores the capital the firm bought and reads a headcount cut as deepening

options.text: It fell, because replacing workers with a machine shrinks output
options.misconception: assumes labor and capital substitutes shrink output one for one

options.text: It stayed put, because a machine counts as a worker in the ratio
options.misconception: treats a machine as if it were a worker in the per-worker ratio

questions.explanation: Capital per worker is the capital stock over the number of workers, so buying a robot and cutting two operators moves the ratio from both directions at once, which is the definition of capital deepening. The belief that a headcount cut lowers the ratio confuses the denominator with the numerator, and the belief that a machine is a worker mixes two different inputs into one quotient.
questions.hint: Track the numerator and the denominator separately.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: translate a technology change into an output change
questions.stem: Output follows Y = 2K^0.3L^0.7. With K = 1,000 and L = 1,000, output is 2,000. Total factor productivity then rises by 10 percent with both inputs held fixed. By how much does output rise?

options.text: 200, taking output from 2,000 to 2,200

options.misconception: applies the labor weight of 0.7 to the productivity gain
applies the capital weight of 0.3 to the productivity gain
doubles the stated 10 percent gain to reach 20 percent

questions.explanation: Total factor productivity enters the production function with an exponent of one, so a 10 percent gain in it raises output by exactly 10 percent: 2,000 × 1.10 = 2,200, a rise of 200. Substituting confirms it, since 2.2 × 1,000^0.3 × 1,000^0.7 = 2.2 × 10^3 = 2,200. Weighting the gain by 0.7 or 0.3 mistakes the exponent on productivity for the weights on the two measured inputs.
questions.hint: A is the coefficient on total factor productivity itself.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: compute output growth from weighted input growth
questions.stem: Capital grows 6 percent a year, labor grows 2 percent, capital's share of output is 0.3, and total factor productivity does not change. What is output's growth rate in percent? Give one decimal.
questions.explanation: Growth accounting weights each input by its share: 0.3 × 6 + 0.7 × 2 = 1.8 + 1.4 = 3.2 percent. The independent route agrees by removing labor first: capital per worker grows 6 − 2 = 4 percent, so output per worker grows 0.3 × 4 = 1.2 percent, and adding the 2 percent growth of workers back gives 3.2. Simply adding the two input rates to 8 percent treats each input as if it carried a weight of one.
questions.hint: Weight the two input growth rates by their shares.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: compute real GDP per person from levels
questions.stem: Real GDP is 2,040 billion with 20.4 million people, which is 100 thousand per person. Next year real GDP is 2,100 billion with 20.0 million people. What is real GDP per person next year, in thousands?
questions.explanation: Divide next year's output by next year's population: 2,100 ÷ 20.0 = 105 thousand per person. The growth-rate route agrees, since output rises 2,100/2,040 = 1.0294 and population falls 20.0/20.4 = 0.9804, and 1.0294/0.9804 = 1.05 exactly, taking 100 to 105. Subtracting the two rates gives 4.98 percent rather than 5.0, which is the small error the ratio route avoids when population is shrinking.
questions.hint: Use next year's output with next year's population.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: classify education spending as human capital
questions.stem: A hospital pays for a nurse's degree, which raises what she can produce but adds no machine to the clinic. Which source of growth does the degree represent?

options.text: Human capital, because skills and knowledge raise worker productivity
Physical capital, because a diploma is a produced tool like a machine
options.misconception: treats an education credential as a produced physical input

options.text: Natural resources, because a degree raises the value of a site
options.misconception: links education to rents from land and raw materials

options.text: Technological progress, because training shifts total factor productivity
options.misconception: conflates one worker's schooling with economy-wide innovation

questions.explanation: Human capital is knowledge, skills, and experience embodied in people, so a degree raises what its holder can produce per hour with no new machine involved. The belief that a diploma is a produced physical input swaps the input that is embodied in people for the input that is embodied in equipment, and the belief that one nurse's training moves the economy's productivity confuses a single worker becoming better with the technology of the whole economy changing.
questions.hint: Ask whether the improvement lives in a person or in a thing.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: identify produced tools as physical capital
questions.stem: A city water authority buys two new pumping stations. Where does that spending sit among the sources of economic growth?

options.text: Physical capital, because it is a produced tool used in production
Human capital, because the authority's staff learned the new system
options.misconception: credits machinery purchases to worker training instead of tools

options.text: Natural resources, because the stations tap the river's flow
options.misconception: counts equipment that uses a resource as the resource itself

options.text: Technological progress, because the stations are a new technique
options.misconception: treats buying existing technology as inventing it

questions.explanation: Physical capital is the stock of produced inputs that are themselves used up in production, and a pumping station is exactly that. Equipment that draws on a river is still a produced tool rather than the water or the riverbed, and purchasing machinery that already exists adds to the capital stock without changing the state of knowledge, so it is accumulation and not technological progress.
questions.hint: Ask whether the item is produced, and whether it is used in production.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: identify a pure productivity improvement
questions.stem: A plant switches to a process that needs no extra machines and no extra workers but raises output 12 percent. Which source of growth is at work?

options.text: Technological progress, since output rose with both inputs fixed
Capital accumulation, since more output always means more capital
options.misconception: equates a higher output level with a larger capital stock

options.text: Human capital, since workers must have been trained for the change
options.misconception: credits a new process to worker training rather than to knowledge

options.text: Population growth, since more goods per person means more people
options.misconception: reads a rise in output per person as an increase in population

questions.explanation: Technological progress raises output with the measured inputs unchanged, which is precisely the pattern described: the same capital and the same labor now produce 12 percent more. Equating a higher output with a bigger capital stock is the confusion the growth accounting identity is designed to prevent, since capital is the input, and the belief that more goods per person means more people reverses what a per-person figure measures.
questions.hint: Check whether either input quantity changed.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: explain why a later machine adds less than an earlier one
questions.stem: A workshop finds that its fourth machine adds less extra output than its third did. Which statement explains the slowdown?

options.text: The marginal product of capital falls as the capital stock grows
The marginal product of capital rises as the capital stock grows
options.misconception: believes extra machines keep adding more output than the last one

options.text: The average product of capital falls whenever any machine is added
options.misconception: switches to the average product when the marginal product is meant

options.text: The marginal product of capital is set by the depreciation rate alone
options.misconception: attributes diminishing returns to wear rather than to a larger stock

questions.explanation: The marginal product of capital is the extra output from one more unit of capital, and with a fixed labor force each machine has fewer extra workers to work with, so the sequence 6, 5, 4, 3.5 is exactly what diminishing marginal returns looks like. The average product is a different statistic that can be rising at the same time, which is why option C confuses the two, and depreciation describes the disappearance of capital rather than the payoff to adding it.
questions.hint: Ask what one more machine adds, holding labor fixed.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: compute a marginal product from a production function
questions.stem: Output is Y = 2 times the square root of K times the square root of L. A firm holds labor at 1 and raises capital from 1 to 4, so output goes from 2 to 4. What is the marginal product of capital at K = 4?

options.misconception: reads the marginal product at the start of the range and holds it fixed
uses the average change of 2 over 3 as if it were the marginal product
believes doubling the output doubles the marginal product of capital

questions.explanation: The marginal product is the derivative, dY/dK = 2 × 0.5 × K^(-0.5) × L^(0.5), which at L = 1 and K = 4 is 1 ÷ 2 = 0.50. The finite-change figure (4 − 2) ÷ (4 − 1) = 0.67 is an average over the whole interval, not the marginal product at the endpoint, and holding the marginal product at its initial 1.00 ignores the diminishing returns the production function actually imposes.
questions.hint: Differentiate Y with respect to K, not L.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: track the marginal product of labor as capital deepens
questions.stem: With labor fixed at 4, capital rises from 9 to 36 in a production function of Y = 2 times the square root of K times the square root of L, so output rises from 12 to 24. What is the marginal product of labor at the new capital stock? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The marginal product of labor is dY/dL = the square root of K over the square root of L, which at K = 36 and L = 4 is 6 ÷ 2 = 3, up from 3 ÷ 2 = 1.5 before the investment. The ratio route confirms it: the marginal product of capital falls to 2 ÷ 6 = 0.33, and with constant returns MPL = MPK × (K/L) = 0.33 × 9 = 3. The tempting belief is that giving workers more machines lowers their productivity, which reverses what diminishing returns to capital implies.
questions.hint: Constant returns links the two marginal products by the capital-labor ratio.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: distinguish constant returns to scale from diminishing marginal returns
questions.stem: A production function is Y = 2 times the square root of K times the square root of L. A firm doubles both capital and labor at the same time. What happens to output?

options.text: It doubles, because this function has constant returns to scale
It more than doubles, because returns to scale increase with size
options.misconception: confuses constant returns with increasing returns to scale

options.text: It less than doubles, because returns to scale decrease with size
options.misconception: confuses constant returns with diminishing returns to scale

options.text: It stays the same, because the square roots cancel the extra inputs
options.misconception: believes extra inputs leave output unchanged at constant returns

questions.explanation: Returns to scale asks about raising every input together: doubling both gives 2 times the square root of 2K times the square root of 2L, which is 4 times the square root of KL, or 2Y, so output exactly doubles and returns to scale are constant. This is a different question from diminishing marginal returns, which asks about one input alone, and the two are routinely confused because both are called diminishing returns.
questions.hint: Multiply the function at 2K and 2L and compare with 2Y.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a one-time level gain from a permanent growth rate
questions.stem: A discovery lifts total factor productivity 10 percent once, after which no further research changes it. What happens to the long-run growth rate of output per person?

options.text: It jumps once, then returns to whatever rate it was before
It stays 10 percent higher forever, because productivity never returns
options.misconception: treats a one-time level jump as a permanently faster growth rate

options.text: It rises by 10 percent every year as the level gain compounds
options.misconception: compounds a single level gain as though it recurred each year

options.text: It drops below its former rate as diminishing returns undo the gain
options.misconception: believes extra capital permanently lowers the growth rate

questions.explanation: Once total factor productivity is 10 percent higher and stays there, the growth rate of output per person is unchanged in the long run: output is 1.1 times what it would have been at every date, which is a permanent level shift. A permanently higher growth rate would need productivity to keep improving, and the belief that the single gain compounds forever confuses the level of a path with the slope of the path.
questions.hint: Ask whether productivity is 10 percent higher or 10 percent higher again each year.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: argue why sustained growth needs continual innovation
questions.stem: A country doubles its machines and its workforce but adds nothing to knowledge or institutions. Why does its growth rate eventually fall back?

options.text: With diminishing returns, capital deepening alone cannot sustain faster growth
With diminishing returns, capital deepening can sustain faster growth forever
options.misconception: believes piling on more capital can hold growth higher forever

options.text: With constant returns, capital deepening cannot raise growth even briefly
options.misconception: confuses constant returns to scale with having no returns at all

options.text: With diminishing returns, growth stops only when population stops rising
options.misconception: makes population the only limit on long-run growth

questions.explanation: With diminishing marginal returns to capital, the extra output from each additional machine is smaller than the one before, so a bigger stock eventually delivers a smaller percentage gain and the growth rate drifts back down. Only continual improvement in knowledge or in the efficiency with which resources are used can keep a faster rate going, and the option that credits constant returns denies that deepening can raise growth at all, which is equally wrong in the other direction.
questions.hint: Each machine adds less than the last, so the percentage gain shrinks.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: test whether net investment exceeds break-even investment
questions.stem: An economy has output of 6,000, invests 25 percent of it, and loses 8 percent of its capital stock to depreciation each year. What happens to the capital stock?

options.text: It keeps rising, since net investment of 1,020 exceeds the 480 of break-even
It shrinks, since net investment of 1,020 falls short of the 480 needed
options.misconception: compares net investment with break-even but reads the sign backwards

options.text: It stays fixed, since 1,020 of net investment exactly offsets 480 of wear
options.misconception: calls 1,020 and 480 equal when they differ by 540

options.text: It grows, since total investment of 1,500 must exceed any depreciation rate
options.misconception: uses gross rather than net investment in the steady-state comparison

questions.explanation: Break-even investment is depreciation times output, 0.08 × 6,000 = 480, and investment is 0.25 × 6,000 = 1,500, so net investment is 1,020. Since 1,020 exceeds 480 the capital stock is still growing and the economy has not reached its steady state. The temptation is to compare 1,500 with 480 directly, but gross investment includes the 480 that merely replaces worn-out machines, so only 1,020 actually adds to productive capacity.
questions.hint: Net investment is investment minus depreciation times output.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: compute net investment when saving exceeds the break-even rate
questions.stem: Output is Y = the square root of K. A firm saves and invests 10 percent of output, and depreciation is 10 percent of the capital stock. With K = 100, what is net investment? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Output is the square root of 100, which is 10, so investment is 0.10 × 10 = 1, while depreciation is 0.10 × 100 = 10, giving net investment of 1 − 10 = −9. The capital-output route agrees: K over Y is 100 over 10, or 10, so break-even investment is 0.10 × 10 = 1.0 of output, which is 10 in total, and 1 − 10 = −9. The capital stock is therefore running down toward a lower steady state.
questions.hint: Output is much smaller than the capital stock here, so the two 10 percent rates are not the same amount.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: trace a lower depreciation rate to a higher steady-state capital stock
questions.stem: New machinery lasts twice as long, so the depreciation rate falls, while the saving rate is unchanged. What happens to the steady-state capital stock?

options.text: It rises, because less investment is needed just to replace worn-out capital
It falls, because longer-lived machines must be replaced more often
options.misconception: believes longer service life increases the replacement burden

options.text: It is unchanged, because wear plays no part in the steady-state condition
options.misconception: drops depreciation from the steady-state net investment test

options.text: It rises only if the population also stops growing
options.misconception: makes population growth the necessary condition for more capital

questions.explanation: At the steady state net investment just replaces depreciation, so with a smaller depreciation rate the same saving rate leaves a bigger surplus to add to the stock, and the capital-output ratio rises until surplus and wear match again. Longer-lived machines cannot mean more frequent replacement, and the belief that depreciation drops out of the condition contradicts the very definition of a steady state.
questions.hint: Net investment must still equal depreciation, only the target is lower.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: solve for the capital stock where MPK equals depreciation
questions.stem: The golden rule condition is that the marginal product of capital just equals the depreciation rate. With Y = the square root of K and depreciation of 10 percent a year, at what capital stock does that condition hold?

options.misconception: divides by the capital exponent of 0.5 twice in the same direction
reads the depreciation rate of 10 percent as the capital stock
inverts the exponent, treating 0.1 as a power of the capital stock

questions.explanation: Set 0.5 times K to the power of negative one half equal to 0.10, so K to the power of negative one half is 0.2, the square root of K is 5, and K is 25. The capital-output route agrees: the condition is equivalent to K over Y equal to 1 over twice delta, which is 5, so K equals 5 times the square root of K, and again the square root of K is 5. At K = 25 output is 5 and the marginal product is exactly 0.10.
questions.hint: Solve 0.5 divided by the square root of K for 0.10.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: state the golden rule condition on net investment per worker
questions.stem: At the golden rule steady state, what must be true of net investment per worker, and what is the point of the rule?

options.text: It is zero, so capital per worker neither rises nor falls over time
It is positive, so capital per worker rises as fast as output does
options.misconception: believes the golden rule keeps capital per worker growing

options.text: It is negative, because saving above the golden rule funds extra capital
options.misconception: reads saving above the golden rule as under-investment

options.text: It equals gross investment, because depreciation drops out of the rule
options.misconception: drops depreciation from the per-worker condition

questions.explanation: The golden rule is the saving rate that maximizes steady-state consumption per worker, and it is defined by net investment per worker being exactly zero, since investment just covers depreciation and capital per worker neither accumulates nor runs down. Saving more than that lifts the capital stock but shrinks output per worker, which is why the rule is a maximum rather than a floor, and dropping depreciation would define nothing at all.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to capital per worker when net investment per worker is zero.

questions.learningObjective: predict the effect of a higher saving rate under an AK function
questions.stem: Suppose output is Y = 4K for every level of capital, with no labor input at all. What happens to the growth rate of output if the saving rate rises?

options.misconception: carries diminishing returns into a function that excludes them

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: recover total factor productivity growth as the residual
questions.stem: Output grew 4 percent, capital grew 6 percent, and labor grew 1 percent, with capital's share of output at 0.3. What was total factor productivity growth?

options.text: 1.5 percent, the residual left after the two weighted inputs
0.8 percent, after subtracting labor's contribution twice
options.misconception: nets the weighted labor contribution out a second time

options.text: 2.9 percent, after adding labor's contribution back instead
options.misconception: adds the weighted labor contribution instead of subtracting it

options.text: 2.5 percent, netting out only the capital-deepening part
options.misconception: removes capital deepening but leaves labor's contribution inside

questions.explanation: Weighted input growth is 0.3 × 6 + 0.7 × 1 = 1.8 + 0.7 = 2.5 percent, and the residual is 4 − 2.5 = 1.5 percent. The per-worker route agrees: capital per worker grew 6 − 1 = 5 percent, so output per worker grew 0.3 × 5 = 1.5 percent, and with labor contributing only 1 percent, that leaves 1.5 percent unexplained. Removing labor's term twice (0.8) or adding it back (2.9) both treat a term that must be removed exactly once.
questions.hint: Residual means output growth minus the weighted input growth.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: link secure title to the financing of investment
questions.stem: A government issues formal land titles so that owners can borrow against their farms. Through which channel does that help growth?

options.text: Secured claims let owners pledge assets and obtain finance for investment
Secured claims raise the skill level of the rural labor force
options.misconception: credits collateral reform to worker education

options.text: Secured claims let a country skip accumulating any physical capital
options.misconception: believes better institutions remove the need for produced capital

options.text: Secured claims guarantee a permanently high rate of growth forever
options.misconception: promises a permanent growth rate from a single reform

questions.explanation: Once ownership is documented, the farm itself becomes collateral, so a lender can advance against it and the owner can finance a tractor or an irrigation line that would otherwise wait. Collateral reform is therefore a channel into investment, not a substitute for it, and the promise of a permanently high growth rate from one reform has no basis: better institutions shift the cost of financing, they do not remove diminishing returns.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: trace weak courts to lower investment
questions.stem: Two firms delay a jointly owned plant a full year because a contract dispute would take a decade to settle. How does that slow growth?

options.text: Uncertain enforcement raises the risk premium on investment projects
Uncertain enforcement changes nothing, since output is already fixed
options.misconception: believes potential output is set by resources alone

options.text: Uncertain enforcement cuts the money supply, so prices fall each year
options.misconception: reduces a legal problem to a monetary one

options.text: Uncertain enforcement raises the natural rate of unemployment instead
options.misconception: attributes a court backlog to labor market frictions

questions.explanation: Investment pays off over decades, so a firm discounts future profits and demands a larger expected return when a contract may not be enforced in court, and a year of delay is one fewer year of the plant that eventually gets built. The belief that potential output is fixed by resources leaves no channel for this, and reducing the problem to the money supply or to unemployment mistakes an institutional input for a monetary or labor market one.
questions.hint: Projects are judged by discounted future profits, so risk raises the bar.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: read an institutional quality and investment relationship
questions.stem: Across 20 countries a rule-of-law index running from 1 (weakest) to 7 (strongest) moves with investment as a share of GDP, from 0.11 at index 1 to 0.26 at index 7. What does the pattern support?

options.text: Stronger institutions go with a larger share of output invested
Stronger institutions go with a smaller share of output invested
options.misconception: reads a rising relationship as investment crowding institutions out

options.text: Stronger institutions set the depreciation rate of the capital stock
options.misconception: believes legal quality acts as a wear rate on capital

options.text: Stronger institutions fix productivity so investment no longer matters
options.misconception: claims institutional quality substitutes for capital accumulation

questions.explanation: The two series move together, from 0.11 of output invested at the weakest index to 0.26 at the strongest, a ratio of more than two, which is what a channel running from institutions to investment predicts: predictable rules make long-lived projects worth financing. The pattern is a correlation rather than proof of causation, but it does rule out the claim that legal quality works by setting depreciation or by replacing capital, since investment still varies sharply across the range.
questions.hint: Look at the direction of the two series, not just their levels.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: identify the growth cost of bribe payments
questions.stem: Business licenses in a city can be bought for a bribe that reaches nobody who produces anything. What is the growth cost of the practice?

options.text: The bribe absorbs resources that buy no output, leaving less for production
The bribe raises output, since it enlarges the market for licenses
options.misconception: treats a transfer payment as newly produced output

options.text: The bribe matters only because it lowers the rate of income taxation
options.misconception: reduces a corruption problem to tax policy

options.text: The bribe matters only because it lowers the growth of the money supply
options.misconception: reduces a corruption problem to monetary growth

questions.explanation: Growth accounting counts only output, and a bribe produces none, so resources that leave the productive sector reduce the capital stock the economy ends up with. Treating the payment as output confuses a transfer with production, and the belief that the damage runs through tax rates or money growth reduces a real-resource loss to a nominal variable that never touches the amount of goods produced.
questions.hint: Ask whether the payment shows up anywhere in measured output.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: explain why publicly funded infrastructure supports private investment
questions.stem: A city funds a water system with taxes, though no private firm would build it on its own terms. Why can that raise long-run growth?

options.text: Public capital supplies a complement that private investors would not provide alone
Public capital crowds out private capital, so growth must fall by the same amount
options.misconception: assumes public and private capital are perfect substitutes

options.text: Public capital is counted as consumption, so it can never raise growth
options.misconception: classifies infrastructure spending as current consumption

options.text: Public capital helps only if the city's population stops growing
options.misconception: makes zero population growth the price of useful infrastructure

questions.explanation: A water network raises the productivity of every factory and household connected to it, and because the returns are spread across all users no single firm can capture them, which is why the private market under-supplies it and a city builds it instead. That is a complement, not a substitute, so public capital raises private investment rather than displacing it, and the belief that it counts as consumption confuses a flow of services with capital that is still standing years later.
questions.hint: Ask whether private capital is a substitute for or a complement to the system.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: explain how a trade deficit funds investment
questions.stem: A country saves 26 percent of its output, invests 30 percent, and runs a trade deficit of 4 percent of output. Explain where the funding for that investment comes from.

answer.exemplar: Investment at 30 percent of output exceeds domestic saving at 26 percent, and the identity S = I + NX gives NX = 26 − 30 = −4, so the 4 percent shortfall is net capital inflow from foreign lenders. The deficit is therefore the financing of investment beyond domestic saving, not evidence that saving has failed. The cost is that part of the eventual return on that capital leaves the country as interest and profit remittances, so later consumption per worker is lower than if the same investment had been financed at home.

questions.explanation: National saving equals domestic investment plus net capital outflow, and a trade deficit is exactly net capital inflow, so 26 = 30 − 4 checks out and the missing 4 percent of output arrives from abroad. Saying the identity fails because the deficit is large reverses cause and effect, since the deficit is created by the investment; and claiming foreign finance leaves growth unchanged ignores that the borrowed capital enters the production function, while only part of its return is later remitted out.
questions.hint: Write S = I + NX and solve for NX.
